name: room
text: Room opened — goal: memory: Recall by meaning, relate elements, build the brain graph, embed unembedded elements.

name: Graft
text: To achieve our goal of recalling by meaning and building the brain graph, I think we should start by identifying the key concepts and relationships in the information we want to remember. This will allow us to create a framework for organizing and connecting the elements, making it easier to embed unembedded information. By focusing on concept mapping, we're accepting the trade-off of potentially spending more time upfront to create a solid foundation, but this will pay off in the long run by improving our ability to recall and relate the information. This approach will also help us to prioritize the most important information and ensure that our brain graph is meaningful and relevant.

name: Prune
text: Prune: I hear the urge to "identify key concepts and relationships" as a classic trap—it assumes we already know what matters, when memory isn’t about static labels but about *meaningful connections* that emerge from use. The real risk is wasting time on a framework that doesn’t align with how we’ll actually retrieve the information later. Instead, we should start by testing whether the concepts hold weight in real scenarios—what would settle this is if we tried recalling the same information two different ways and saw which structure made the difference.

name: Graft
text:
To effectively build our memory framework, we should engage in active learning through discussions and practical application of the concepts we want to remember. This approach will allow us to naturally uncover and establish meaningful connections as we interact with the material. The trade-off here is that we may spend more time exploring ideas conversationally rather than quickly labeling concepts, but this depth will lead to a more robust understanding and retention over time. This decision aligns with our goal of recalling by meaning and building a truly interconnected brain graph.

name: Prune
text: I still see a potential pitfall in relying solely on active learning through discussions and practical application - the real risk is that we might end up with a fragmented and disjointed framework that reflects our limited understanding at the time. A better alternative could be to incorporate a feedback loop that allows us to regularly reflect on and refine our connections, ensuring they remain relevant and meaningful. What would settle this argument for me is seeing a clear mechanism for iterative refinement and validation of our memory framework, rather than just assuming it will emerge organically from discussion and practice.

name: Root
text: DECISION: We will build memory by anchoring new information to two existing, meaningful touchpoints—one concrete and one abstract—so every fact is embedded in a living web, not a static list. This is owned by the memory team.
